New Wm. ton Mite.—At the recent annual meeting of the American Dairymen's Association two new tests for milk were explained and illustrated by Professor G.C. Cald- well, of Cornell University. The first wan by an Instrument based OH the opacity of milk. A small amount of milk is pot in the bottom of it tithe, having an inner tube, with a scale lined off in black. The lines are invisible. Water is poured in until the lines are distinct enough to be counted. The upper part of the tube has number. showing on one ride the percentage of water added and on the other the per- ! centage of fats. Many analyses had attested the approxi- I mate accuracy of this test. Another test was with a tube, ! in which an equal portion of milk and ether was shaken to- , nether until the mixture was et-en and uniform. Then the some measure of alcohol as was taken of milk war added to the mixture, and the whole shaken into a uniform MASS. The tube W., then net in water at 104 deg. for live minutes, ' and afterwards plunged in water at 66 deg. for five minutes. This completed a separation of the fat of the milk, which stood in a clear maw on the top. The lower line of the fat stood at 26 on the scale numbered on the glass, and the upper line at 15. The difference, 11, was taken, and refer- ence to a table determined this to indicate 319 per cent, of fat. The milk war pronounced a good simple. This led to a discussion as to what should he considered • fair atandanl of milk. In England, it was said, 2/, i.er cent, of fat is con- sidered sufficient, and in some other European countries 3il is required. There Ix a corrmponding variation as to the • required amount of minis. There is in, standard adopted in America. Professor Engelliarder analysis of Syracuse milk has led him to accept 21 percent. of fat am a fair amount. It was thought at the meeting a certain amount of solids and fats should be fixed upon as a stand:int for the supply of city milk, and a committee of Ave was appointed to memorialise the Legislature on the subject. The amount of fat in milk and in cream varies greatly, but the solids nut fat" are very constant. In this country public analysts following Professor J. Alford Wanklyn hone adapted 9-2 solid, not fat as the lowest standani for pure milk.

div.p: HEALTHY PIGS AND HOW TO REAR THEW

I often read with regret, hut not surprise, of diseas—eipigs —and know, from extensive experience, that it is avoidable. For none years I kept large numbers, until, owing to their proximity to the house, they lecame a nuisance to tny growing family. But, although I hail no inituy, and closely packed, they were ono:taken:illy timidly—and I will now give my reasons for their being no. I was frequently told that owing to my having SO many (some 2fail there would be diseene, but I felt perfectly sure it would not be so' seeing the cause for disease was not present. Pigs have a desire to huddle together, and they. thus create a putrescent attnosphere, esp i ecially fmt soft straw ; and that is why farmers prefer strong reedy whmt straw, frequently changed, to admit air under them. In iny .121,! they were always on sparred wooden floors, the spars being 3in. wide, with an interval between each spar,and a deep pk under thein, so that the change of temperature caused by the heat of their balks and their breathing, Is continually • circulating and changing the atmosphere amend, under, land above them—there should be, of course, escape open- ings for the heatiel air in the upper part of the stye or shed. !There can thus be no stagnation of air--so fetal to limn and beast. In cold vreather they may be very closely packed or ' enclosed, en they have no woollen jacket, and horno long and strong bristles, like the hogs of cold countries. (Amuse the urine all falls between the spars, and the solid they generally deposit in one corner. In hoe, summer weather I was must successful in fatten- , tug hogs, without fear of fever (freouently no timtruci.ive). ! Inn shel that would hold forty or fifty (sparred floor. with , deep pit under it), I turned on my jet, m from a fire-ergine, I and in ale,, minutes they were all washed clam, and re- ! frothed, and would rub their skins as clean as the back of !my hand. A fresh lot, coining in from tnarket dirty, were wort cleaned under a shower of 60 gallons per mittute.Thom , who prefer putting a little draw on the hoards in winter can do so—the urine will still run through, and the air ch.- late., which is the great desideratum. Boarded floors have been long used in Essex for fattening calves, experience • proving the advantage of the practice. Almost all animals In best on sparred tioors--from bullinik too rabbit. They greatly economise our straw, and net it free for ntirket or „ for food. It is lamentable to see pig mismanagement. Bur. ' rowing in immure, getting heated, and then by exposure ' catchirg cold and lung dismse (heaves), or fever. Pigs are grom feeders, and soon poison a notecireulating atmosphere. ! The labourer's pig, being alone, escapes the danger of close • company, and consequent puisonixt atinimphere. I have fattened hundreds of cattle on spured doors with- out a particle of straw or any sweeping of doors, the excreta, all passing between the spars to the pit under them. I once load twelve white cattle . thme spars from the time they , were six months old until sold fat id two years old,and they I were always clean :Ind healthy. In feet, from calves until full-grown for the butcher, my cattle were constantly on I sparred doors. They always fattened an quickly and grew as well as those on straw in covered yards, and were , especially healthy. This system of sparred floor. is a most ! important one where straw in dear and scarce,aleo where the ' excreta are washed on to the land IT selvage, and mortice- larly as a prevention of disease. Sparred doors economise , much labour. It is well to put animals on them when 1 young. I have fattened sheep on them very successfully. • Shoop require more ventilation than hairy animals. It is worth noting that sheep on straw 111,iinr cover do not get foot rot, and can do with little straw ; but in open yards, en- pored to rainfall, they will get bad feet unless very fre- i quently littered. Urine does not rot the feet. When far- mers give up the belief that Mr. Mechi is a mere theorist, it will he better for their pockets, and then I shall be much gratified. The opening between the spars may be aroerdime to the size of the .nni,oaln u quarter inch of opening would permit free circulation of ale; one and a half inch is a good size for cattle.—J. J. If a writer in the Jr, red, a short time ago, is to be be- lieved, " Cromwellian, Frodsharn,' will find the remains of the great Protector at Newburgh, in Yorkshire. The writer, after giving an interesting sketch of rho home at Conwold of the huinomus larwretice Sterne, the author of "Tris- tram Shandy," relates a singrilar story in connection with the history of the reerkhnce of Sir George Wombwell at Newburgh, in the same parish., in the North Riding of York- shire. The writer say,--" In Sir George Wombwell's pri- vate snuggery. behind the stnoking-mmt, where he transacts his businms, are many reins ef the &den time—early local newspapers, advertisements of the flying coaches, which did the dishince been ondon and York in forty-eight hears, and—far more precious than these—several letters of Sterne to his patron, Lord Fauconberg, turning mostly ou London gomip and passing events, both treated after the inimitable inanner of the author of the • Seutimental Journm•.' Sterne is a hind of tutelary spirit of Coxwold, and there are few more agreeable ways of passing a morning than in making a pilgrimage to his shrine. Turning down the road, we pass the well-known village inn, the only thatched house in Cox- wold, and arrive id the curious old church, with its hexa- gonal tower, and pulpit celebrated as that front which Yorick's sermons were delivered. A little farther on, on the opposite side of the way, is Shandy Hall, the house in which the ' Sentimental Journey ' and ' Tristram Shandy' were written. It is no longer the vimrage, and has, in fact, been divided into two workmen's cottages. The rooms occupied hv Sterne, however, still preserve their original features. The yew-tree, too, under which meditation and composition were done in summer time, is stil! leech and green an the memory of the delightful writer. who love,' to sit under it. There is, howeve-, a mightier memory than that of Lmrenee Sterne associated with Newburgh. In the long gallery is no glass case contain- ing the saddle, holsters, iMgols, hi, and bridle of 'tire greatest prince who ever ruled in England.' llie saddle and holster-cases are by no 1111,1aS i.f Puritan simplicity, being of crimmn velvet hn.vilvr,oi,roi,lccol in gold. The pistols are of portentous, length, nod very thin in the barrel, and the bit is a cruel one, with the tremendous cheek-pieces common two centuriers ago—huddle. the Lord Protector liked his horse, like his Roundheads, well in hand. Not quite oppo- site to them relics, hangs the portrait cot a lady clad in dark green and denaurenms. This serious-looking dame is Mary Cromwell, wife of the second Lord Fanconberg, and daughter of the Lord Protector. It Was she who, with keen womanly instinct, aharpened yet more by Mid affection, foresaw that, the Restoration once achieved, the men who had fied before (Oliver at !iambs and Worcester would not allow his bones to rest in Westminster. At dead of night hie corpse was removed from the *ult in the Abbey, and that of some member of the undistinguished crowd sub- stituted for it. In solemn secrecy, the remains of him of whom it was said, `lf not a kiog, he wee a roan whom , it was good for kings to have among them,' were con- veyed to Newburgh, where they yet repose; the insane fury of the Royalist ghouls, who hung thr supposed body of Cromwell as well as tlmt of Ireton on the gal lows tif 'Tyburn, having thus been cheated of its noblest prey. The tomb of Cromwell occupies the end of a narrow ehamber at the head of a flight of Keep 31Airn, :Ind is an enormous ma. of stone- work built and cemented into tire walls, apparently with the object of making it impregnable. Them is no reason to doubt the truth of this story, pre,..7v.el in the liellasyse family for two centuries air Ia mi gt..c. iii, not a legend, hut a genuine Mem of hoMly his•ery. and implicitly Se- on the spot. It is needl..ss in say that the over- curious have again and again begged the lords of Newburgh to have the tomb opened; but this request has met with in- variable refusal, even when in ogfered irolioromont illmtrious personages. 'No, no,' observes Sir George Wombwell, heartily as ever, hut 'trite firmly, •w, do not make, show of our great relative's tomb, end it Aar not Ise opened. In thin part of Yorkshire we no more dig up our remote great:- uncles than we sell our grandmotht •s. The Protector's bonee shall rest in pea, at least for my tone." If this singular statement is true, it knocks in the hem' altogether the generally accepted story that Cromwell eras, with Ireton and Bradshaw, buried at the foot of the gallows at Tyburn. 111,01<1e,.

The condemned man was brorrxht born the fortress to the place of execution strapped in • sitting position toe high seat en a black painted vehicle, and pliced with his hack to the horses. A placard, hearing tie words "State criminal," was rrttacired to his dress. A tonna of Cossacks escorted the ear. The scaffold was: er. cted in the Sitneonofsky Plain, and was surrounded by infantry formerl in hollow square. On the way to the ' scaffold, and after reaching it, Mlarletaky appeared quite calm, evens iling occasionally. Alter the sentence had been read the prisoner turned and bowed on all sides to the people, and just before being delivered over to the hang- man, spoke a few words to the priest and binned the cross. AFGHANISTAN. A Daily News Lahore telegram says if the arrangements for a peaceful settlement of Afghanistan fail, the spring cam- paign will include a flying column to Charikar. At the nod of Marche force for Koorum will march through Zurtnut,to Ghazni, co-operating with a strong column from Candela., General Robertn moving in a south-westerly direction, and blocking the tihusni roads towards l'urkestan. The Inger and Koorunt forces are now deficient in transport. The /away Clororzi,la's Allababad correspondent learns on sound authority from Cabot that the made lying south-west of Argandi are again closed by masses of hostile trihesmen. The southern road is the main one from Cabal to °Muni, which in connequently again blocked for the present against the approach of General Roberts. The Times.Cabul corres- pondent mys that the situation has not materially changed. The eltief interest of the situation lies in the course Sinter Maher Ftahman may decide upon. Winter is new decidedly on the wane, and the occupation of Sharper will probably not be prolonged beyond this month. The brigade in the Bala Blew will, of coulee, continue to hold that inmortant position. A Times Caadahar telegram says all is quiet in' that district. The health of the troops is very good. A Times Calcutta telegram says General Roberta estimate/. the ' force opposed to on as at no titan exceeding 60,000, and he reckons their losses at about 3,000 killed and wounded. A Maaclard Cologne telegram save news has reached St. Peters- burg from Cobol that Abdul- Rahman Khan has summoned a meeting of the sirdars and khans of North Afghanistan to Maitnene, Ms present 'dace 4 residence, with a view to their proclaiming him Attlee, Mabomed Jon has bean invited.

Gentlemen,—Her Majesty's MiMsters have at length decided to terminate the existence of tine Parliament, and to give the constituencies of the United Kingdom an oppor- tunity of pronouncing their verdict upon the ism. which have been no long and so fully discuseed in Parliament and throughout the country. I hasten, therefore, to redeem the pledge which I gave now n.rly nine months ago, and to ask dm elec.rs of North-east Lancashire, by returning me as one of their member% to renew the connection which many years since existed between Ohm constituency enrl my- self. I ask them thus to give a peaof of the confidence which. eel believe, they feel in the principlen of the party to which I belong, and their approval of the policy which in the present Parliantent I have consistently but unsuccess- fully advocated. The l'rime Minister has stated in his letter 00 11,0 Lord-Lieutenant of lrelmd the 180095 Which , in his ojoinion, the country will be called upon to decide. I seek to evade 110 issue which the Government cen raise but it ie necessary that they should be plainly stated, and that others it Welt he has avoided should be brought before you. I know of no par.y teloMh "challenges the ex- pediency of the Imperial character of this realm." I know of none who have "attempt.l to enfeehle our coloni. by their policy of decomposition." flour colonies are at this moment more loyal to toe throne, onore attached to the con- nection with the mother country, more willing to undertake the common rtspongbility and burdens which must be borne by all menibers of 0 great empire tllt,, ot any former time, it is due to the foot that under the guidance of Liberal mato,- men they have received institutions of completc .elf-goo-ern. ment, and have learned to recognise the treth that entire dependence en imperial assistance for their protection and defence in not compatible with their dignity or freedom. No patriotic purpose is in my opinion, gained by the use of the language of exaggeration in describing Otto Irish agitation for Ilmee Rule. I believe the demand no described to he impracticable; and considering that any concession or appearance of concession in this ditection would be mischie- vous in its effecta to the prosperity of Ireland, as well as that of England and Scotland, I have consistently opposed it in office and in opposition, and I shall continue to oppose it. The agitation has existed during the whole of the continu- ance of this Parliament. It bas been treated by the Govern- ment until now, if not with indulgence, w ith indifference and the ,ortempt to rouse motional jealousies and reawaken national animosities by descriptions of dangers "worse than pestilence and famine,' appears to on to be unnecesgory unwise. This agitation must he !net, not by passionate ex- aggeration, but by firm and consistent resistance, combined with the proof that the Imperial Parliament is able and willing to grant every reasonable and just demand to the Irieh people for equal lawn and inetitutions. • We have willingly and without referenee to party con- siderations co-operated with the Government in the measurer which they have prongsed for extending to the Irish people. without distinction of religious creed, the advantages of in- termediate and univereity education. The efforts of the late Government in this direction were defeated by a combi- nation of which the party now in power formed the pi inci- pal eletnent. It would net have been for us to have formed a similar combination forthe purpose of embarrassing the Government. but we preferred to assiet in the passing of measures which, though in our opinion inadequate in glue respects, and not calculated to provide a final settlement of the question, at least raven prouf to the Irish people of the desire of all parties in Parliaonent to meet a re.onable Irish demand. Much, howevg, remaine to be done in removing thow inequalitio.r of the law which still exist to the iliarcl- vantage of Ireland, ere we can hope that the Irish people will be convinced of the just impartiality of the Parliament of the United Kingdom, Lord Beaconsfield claims that Her Majesty's ministers baye maintained the peace of Europe, which be justly describe. "as nec.eary to llie welfare of the civilised world,' but they could not prevent—even if tlteir policy did not cauw—a war in the East of Europe. The ascendency of England h. been claimed in circular., but it has been nor- rendered in secret conventiens. in the aggrandisement of Russia and the destruction of the integrity and the inde- pendence of the Turkish empire. The declared object of their policy has been &merged. The settlement of the Eastern quegion. which the Government claimed to hare effect,l, rested in a nolin degree on the Anglo-Turkish Con- vention, which stipulated for the reform of Turkish rule in Asia Minor. In the time which has elmwed since that con- vention was signal no progress whatever lug leen mgle towards giving effect to its provisione. Her Majesty's Minister. themselves will not deny that all the remonstrances they have addressed to the l'orte, and all the efforts they have made to reform the Government, have totally failed. and the convention itzelf still remain • dead letter. We were told two verge ago by the Government Chat the Greek question was settled, and that Greece had obtained all that a reasonable Power could demand in the frontier defined by the protocol of Berlin ; but Greece has obtained nothing, and that question, which still disturbs F.astern Europe, is as far Irene a solution as ever. Than the policy has failed, but the immense responsibilitiee incurred by this country re- main—responsibi litim in return for which the acquisition of CypiedlB, which adds nothing to the military strength of the nation, affords no adequate compensation. In Africa her , Majesty's Ministers hare drifted into a.OOO which thee did I not maction, and which they deplore—a war which he' brought no honour and no advantage in return for the blood and treasure which have been spent. In Afghanistan then I have created a near which has d.troyel orotion,fl,retronottbo ' and independence and friendship of which they declared, in common with their predecessors, to be important for tloe safety ofithe frontier of India_ The dower of the Indian army and the resources rd India are gill employed in guard- ing the ruins which they have made and in repressing doe anarchy they hare let loow. SIR S. NORTHCOTE'S ADDRESS TO THE ELECTORS OF NORTH DEVON. The following is the full text of the address ,d the Right Hon. Sir Stafford H. Nrthcote to the electors of the tiorth division of the county of Devon TO THE ELHCTOHS Or NORTH DEVON. Gentlemen,—Her Majesty hag declared In r grae:ms in- [whorl to dissolve the present Parliament. dinloll I shortly haveoccasion to solicit at your hands a renewal of the trust winch you have done me the honour to confide in me as y.our.r.epregentative.

--Tfie.ilitration of the Parliament now about to be dissolved has bon long, but its age it not to be measured by the num- ber of years for which it has eat so much as by the im- portance of the events which have occupied it during the term of its existence, and the magnitude of the hones 1 which it Isas boen called on to decide. Throughout. period of no cotnmon difficulty and anxiety, it has upheld the honour tithe country, and has vindicated its claims to ite! proper rank and Intl nonce amongst the nations of the world.' Though it has not escaped the captious criticism of. certain number of politicians within an -I without its walls, it has received at the hands of the nation a generous recognition of its patriotic aims, and its courageous firmness in support of [hone great inten•ets which El British Parliament has it in charge to maintain. fin foreign and colonial and its domestic policy have all been animated by the same spirit, and the same determination to uphold at once the grmtness, integrity, and the constitution of the empire, and to knit together the various races who own the sovereignty of the Queen, and the varionsclassee which conWitute the strength of the people. It has laboured to avert war, and, where that haa not been poteible, it has successfully ertrivon to limit its range, and to prevent com- plications which would have been alike menacing to the particular interests of this country, and to the general peace of Europe. It has emphatically proclaimed the national determination to maintain, strengthen, and defend our great colonial and Indian empire. It has earnestly pro- moted measures for the advancement of the true interests of Ireland, while it has iceattily resisted proposals, however plausible, tending to weaken, or even to dinnlve, the ties winch bind together the inetnle, of the United Kingdom. In its domestic legislation, it has kept in view the import. once ef aiming at the general good of the community, and of doing strict pudica between apparently conflicting in- Mreste, without sacrificing the welfare of one clone to the claims or the prejudices of others. At the same time, it has been on itei guard against the danger of attempting to re- model our ancient institutions in accordance with theoretical ideas unsuited to the national character. Croided by these principles, it has been able to effect substantial improve- ments in many of the laws directly or indirectly affecting the great industrial clean., bath in their relatmn to one another and in the amelioration of their social, moral. and

The filLITICial policy which it has supported has heen with a bitterness easy to be understood, but which con tody be illKitll4l upon the tuneable hypothesis that it is the duty of a finance minister, when the meessitics of the State compel hint. to provide tor additional expenditure, and to to c. in the mann., most oppessive to the taxpayera, without regard oilier to the character of the expenditure or to the circumstances of the country. I cannot attempt within the limits of this address CO deal with the extra- ordinary misrepresentation of financial facts which have been industriously put forth by come of the Opposition of the present Government. I will content myself with point- ing out that after a period of almost unexampled commercial depression and of gmve ag-ricultural losses...lntim., which we have had to incur the expense of defending our interests in three different quarters of the globe,the taxation of the count ry is lighter than in almost any year previous to the accession of the present Government to power, while the real amount of the national debt stanols new at Da millions below the sum at which we found it. The Crimean war added upwards of 40 millions to the debt, and left the taxpayer subject to an income tax of Is. 4d. mn the pound, besides heavy imposts OIJ the necessaries of life. The war into which but for a decided policy we should proluth:y have been drawn, would have been even more burdensome. both to the taxpayer of the day and to our posterity.

I trust. gentlemen, that the period of our anxiety is now drawing to a close. and that it will be in the power of the next Parliament to carry on the work of social and domestic improvement with undivided energies. Should the corning elections result in a renewal of the national confidence in the present Ministry. it will be our earnest ..zol,avour to show ourselves worthy of that confidence he pnreuing the same lineeof policy as those which / have briefly indicated.which have been maintainel by or in the sight of tide empire and of the word, and on which the electors of Of United King- i dom are now called to pronounce. I an, gentlemen, your obedient wervant, (Signed) STAFFORD H. NORTHCOTE.

Lownow, THURSO.. Gentlemen,—l heartily rejoice that the time has at length Arrived when you will be called upon to decide by your votes bether you approve or whether you condemn the manner in which the Government of this great empire has during these last years been mrried on. This, gentlemen, is well although, by a striking departure from established practice. . which must muse great inconvenieree, a session opened by her Majesty with the regular anomie.- went ,d its annual work ii, without the occurrence of any Pwliamentary difficulty, for the first time in our history to be interrupted after a few weeks boo li.- to the electioneering address which the Prime Minister has 'Mitred, an attempt is made to work upon you- fears by dark allusions to the repeal of the Union and the abandonment of the colonies. Gentleman, those who vll- - the Union with Ireland were the party that main- tained there an alien Church, and unjust land law, and franchises inferior to our 01.11, and the true supporters. of the Unim are those who firmly uphold the sureinr authority of Parliament, but exercise that authority to bind the three nations by the in dissoluble tie of literal and equal laws. A. to the colonies. It is by these measures that the coloniee have leen bound in affection to the empire ; and the authors of them can afford to smile at baseless insinuations. Gentle - Ow true purpose of thew terrifying cci, nations ii to hide from view the acts of the Ministry and their eft,' ! upon the character and condition of the country. To these I wi!l now begin to draw your attention. With three wore years and ten upon my head, I feel the , irksomenes.s of the task ; bntln tech. crisis no mau should shrink from meet which his duty may make and Ins strength !allow. div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, MARCH 13, 1880.
THE DISSOLUTION AND LORD BEACONS-
FIELD'S
LTTLECI

After all that Its been said and written during the lad few weeks respecting the intentions of the Go• vestment, the announcement of the dittoingon has come at a time when it was least expected. Lord Beaconefield's alleged design of appealing to the country on the question of obstruction haring been , trustratwl by the conduet of the Opposition, and of x the Home Rulers themselves, the House of Commons seemed to have been settling down for serious work, when suddenly the ei ord goes forth that the end has come. Liberals and Conservatives alike were to some extent taken by aurpriee, but in no instance that has I, come under our notice has the Liberal party been found unprepared. In nearly every instance where the seats are at present occupied by Conservatives there are Liberal candidates ready to take the field, so that in counties and boroughs alike the great electoral battle promises to become general all along the line. At Warrington the Liberal party were mingularly active, and Mr. Meldinniete address, posted on the , walls throughout the borough emly on Tuesday 4 morning, was probably the first that wm issued i.nny part of the kingdom. The Prime Minister adopta the ! expedient of appealing to the country in • letter ad- dressed to the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, end this is done obviously for the purpose of attracting attention ' to the demand for Home Rule, and which Lord Beaconefield craftily insinuates is a measure which derives more or lem support from the Liberal party. Nothing can be more unfair or dieingenuoue than the attempt that Lord Beaconsfield makes to chow that the Liberal party are the encouragers of Home Rule, and also that they have attempted to "enfeeble our colonies by their policy of decomposition." Who are the Home Rulers amongst the prominent member, of the Liberal party? Where can it be shown that Mr. Gladstone er the Marquis of Hartington or Sir W. Harcourt or any prominent Liberal even amongst the rank and file of the Liberal party has ever advocated the giving up of the colonim, with the exception, indeed of Mr. Lowe? The manifold° of the Prime Minister ix a gross piece of exaggeration and misstate- ment from beginning to end, and the country will hail with delight the Marquis of Hartington'e reply tom unscrupulous an attack, and hie ablevindica- lion of the policy of the Liberal party with regard to Ireland. Lord Beaconsfield labours to make English- men believe that "the power of England and the pea. of Europe" will depend on the verdict of the country at the coming general election being in his favour. His audacity is truly marvellous, as it) the attempt he makes to turn the patriotic feeling of Englishmen to account at the elections that are upon ua. It is, perhaps, a rather unfortunate circum- stance that the Government at the present time owes its majority for the most part to English borough and county constituenciee, while Ireland sends a majority of Home Rulers to represent her, and Wales and Scotland aro largely Liberal. We all know hoer the Government majocitim in the English counties have been obtained, but be that as it may, the fact that England as at present represented is more con- servative than any other portion of the United Kingdom, encouras-es the notion Lord Beaconsfield wishes to propagate that the Conservative party is the only true and patriotic party opposed to the 'decomposition' of the empire. At home, policy of repression and force in dealing with domestic or national grievances or complaints; abro id a policy of constant interference in the affairs of Emopean natione in order to maintain the "amen. daney of England." These are the battle cries with whith the Prime Minister leads hie followers to the booths on this 07=40n. But in the mean- time what the country was looking for was a Liberal programme of a foreign and domestic policy that would present an agreeable contrmt to that which we see fore-shadowed in themanifeatoe of the Tory Minister, and that would recommend itself to the people of England, Scotland, and Ireland alike. Lord Harting- ton has supplied that want. His able and etatesman- like addreee is a splendid vindication of the past policy. and of the undotibtfal patriotism of the Liberal party ' tlel well att an earnest of what may be expected, of it in the future. Lord Beaconsfield hae had the execrably bad taate—we had almost said the extreme wickednem—to make use of Ireland's unfortunate poeition at the present moment as a party cry. The Liberal leaders need not be afraid to take up the gage of battle no defiantly thrown down to them. Mr. Forster, in his address to the theaters of ' Bradford, has aim given a very effective reply to a por- I tion of Lord Beaconsfield's mandeetoc when he says, "While I am determined to maintain the union with Ireland, I am also determined to do what in me lies to make Irishmen as anxious as Englishmen and Scotchmen to preserve that union." It is • libel upon English patriotism to say that it can have no sympathy tot Irish grievames, and no with to adopt any other means for removing Irish discontent than by adopting measures of coercion, and pertinaciously refusing all requeste for even making an inquiry into the came, of such discontent.

ARBITRATION IN THE IRON TRADE. Sir,—Tlie eontroversy hot w elm Balltongs "and Mr. James Capper is rather of a painful nature, and I do not think h would be wiae on my part to prolong it but 1 mnnot help observing what a pity it is that men of" Balltongs "typo can be found to vilify men of the character of Mr. J. Capper, who is, or nearly so, a stranger in the town, but who came down at the express wish of a few to explain the nature and character of the new sliding scale by which our wager§ are regulated iill• he done any wrong in no doing ? If we, I venture to say as a worktnan, had not men like Mr. Capper to speak out for us, both at depremed times and at revi al in trade, when they do come, we should stand a very poor chance of competing with the cunning and subtlety of our employer, whose cunnind and subtlety is backed out by men of the 0 Balltongs" type. I question the etatement he made in reference to his using them. Perhaps, Mr. Editor, In used to do, but now rinds a more profitable employment: lent if he does one them and is dependent upon them, or tbe use of than, for the bread he eats, then let him like a matt, attack Mr. Capper in an honest manner, open, fair, and anove board. He has no occasion te be afraid of his eituation. Oh, no! We have good employers whowon't take advantage. &sides, there is plenty of work in the country now, no there is no fear of starving. Don't be afraid Balltongs," but come on liken man : put your name to the next epistle and tel us know who you are.-1 an. ' CID CAP.

Sir,—Will you permit me a short space just to reply to Mr. Ciapper's letter, which appeared in your issue of Satur- day last' I have notquestioned the principled arbitration. What 1 question is the wisdom of joining ourselves with the South Staffordshire Board, and, having epent part of my life in the ironworks of South Staffordshire and put in War- rington, ' 3111 bald enough to think I am a better judge than Mr. Capper, for not only 1.9 he not worked here, but he knows nothing of our ways of working or the prices paid for the different classes of labour outside puddling. That being no, how can he tell or what is beet for us? With regard to &laming and mierepresenting Mr. Capper, I did neither. I simply asked a few ',lain goodie., which he, being unable to answer, is pleased to call abuse. I stated a few plain, positive facts, which he cannot dispute. These he calla inisrepresenmtion. I leave your readers to judge between us. 1 must ask Mr. Capper not to lose his temper, and he careful to tell the truth. Ile says I got nothing. I got Is. &I.; and to bulk about not aaking for it eiraply shows he known nothing of the system pursued here, or he would know it is not necessary to ask. And, maybe, if the South Board hail been in the South Sea Islands, we should have got more in Warrington without asking than they have in Staffordshire with very big asking. 1 do not believe in intik., 0e locksout. My breast depends upon my labour. I do not live by scheming, but by karst work, and when I strike I starve ; but I have heard of men who live by scheming, who until recently were very fond of advocating strike,. But it doesn't pay now. I do not think Mr. Cap- per believes in arbitration no much as I to. I understand him to Pay it is goal so far, but if they push it too far, "thee," I want to know what comes after "then." He doer not finish the sentence. floes he mean etrikes? If Mr. Capper knew all about the many cautes of depression, why did he agitate the minds of men by telling them they were entitled to Be. when he knew he could not prove any such claim? Will Mr.Capper tell us—lst. Hire have not the mme foreign competition now as formerly, and if the high prices are not the cause of it ? find. If the producing power of this end all other countries income greater than once? 3rd. Where have the strikes and lockouts occurred since 1871? Certainly not in Warrington; he has been absent from an. 4th. If arbitration is all we need, why is he now trying to get up a union? Arbitrators ehould decide upon facts, and so union. however strong, ought to influence an award. In conclusion, I would say we do not want any board. We have for years worked peaceably, and a good feeling exists between or and our employere and, if we ever eel leaders to meet and discuss with our employers, we tan tind them in Lancanhire, and need not go south. or north for them. We need no paid agitators to mono ill-feeling between an mid' our employers; and I would advise Mr. Capper not tocome here at the request of a very few dimatisfied men, but wait until the majority of Ca men need hie service., and then there will be no need to send round the hat for expensee. I thankfully decline the invitation to meet Mr. Capper. I have not the ready tongue, and I do not care about public- . houm company ; and I think it will be much mote to the profit of nny own clam if ntat.re which affect their welfare are published in your valuable paper, no that men can read them by their own firmide, consider them carefully, and be their own judge. We want facto that will bear the test of reason, not big worm and erroneous statements BALLTONGS. SCARLET PF,VER AT LYMM.

Sir,—The Local Board and Dr. Fox have now made their statements in defenCe, or in explanation, of their conduct. which appears in last Saturday's E..r. vlnirter, with reference I to the outbreak of *cadet fever in Lymm, and so we are one step neater too final judgment on the question of their rmpective or mutual responsibility in relation to it. Now to help the public to come to a sound decision on this , subject, let us suppose a case and try their conduct by it. Let us suppose an outbreak of scarlet fever—primary cause utterly unknown—in one of our numerous Lvnim mansions, aid let us suppose that Dr. Fox was, not the medical officer of health of the district, hut a respectable village practi- tioner, called in to attend to it. His tirst direction to the mother would undoubtedly have been to isolate the patient, , to separate it from every other niember of the fancily except , herself and one of the nurses, and themost convenient room in the mansion to carry out the plans would be set :mart for it. Probably he would intimate the great desirability, in enter to remove all danger from the others, that, under the circum- stance, the rem of the children, wdli a nurse and goyim-new, should go and learn their daily lesson, at the sea-sule till the little sufferer recovered; when the sick room and all its furniture would be disinfected, the ceiling lime-washed, and the walls freshly papered : and the convalesce., with its mother and nurse, would go to the sea-side also, till all possible danger 1.14. over. Next, we will Suppose the same Dr. Fox was called in to attend another case en scarlet fever, the child of a working man, but living comfortably and respectably in a good four-roomed cottage, of which Mr. Dixon'n or Mr. Appletun's may be taken as a specimen. It is manifest that the doctor could not recommend the adop- tion of any such I,lans here as he clid in the mansion ; though the same plan as near as could be was equallY necessary if the fever was to be kept from spreading. go to make the parallel complete, we will suppose that there icon hospital over the way to which the workingman, the father of the Sick child. ham subscribed for years, for the eery purpose of protecting his family against infection in such eases. And we will suppose that the doctor, though he knows all this, quietly shuts his eyes to the fact, and allows the disease to run its course through the family, but to show that he is , really doing something to save the healthy children in the bowie from taking the infection, send. his servant man to pour a bucketfull or two of carbolic acid into the grids and misers round gamut the house! I ask, would not such con- duct under such circumstances sound something very like insanity? And if the children died, us in the case of the Booths, one after another, till the whole family of tive were swept away, W4llllll not such • doctor, as we have been sup- peeing, be justly regarded in the public opinion of the dis- trict as morally responsible for the consequences? And let to some large extent thew suppositioto Gaffs, except so for an relates to Dr. Fox's private personal medical connection with them, represents the facto of this Lymm outbreak of scarlet fever. Though Dr. Pox was not the medical practitioner M attendance on any of the casea, he admits that he. she medical officer of health for the district, knew of these cases, for he says, an reported in your paper. "that them was not a single rase of Hitless from scarlet fever that heal been known to the medical men which hml nal eame nosier the notice of the Board "; and therefore must ham come under his own. And we must not for a momsnt forget that he is the Medi- cal Officer of Hmlth appointed far the purpose, as far AA may be, of preserving the district from such outhrmks. And he and the ',Val Board had the power, within their own hands, of leg ,Ily and orderly opening the door of the hospital for the reception of all the victims who hare died. 'Phe only way. be it remembered, by which a family in a cottage I can be preserved from this infection is—just as in the cam of the family in the tnansion—hr isolation, by separation of the patient (mm 11,,. other meridiem of the family. Nature knows no distinction between rich 01141 poor in such eases. And this separation can only be carried out in the Con. 41 the poor man's family by sending the sick child be the hospital and leaving the remainder of the family at home. Now the hospital is there, rented he the Local Board for this very purpose of saying the public from such outbreaks, and pee, until nine deaths from scarlet fever had occurred in Lwmin, that is. until the disease had been allowed to So scrd I-road-mat over the village, there was not a

single case sent to the hoepital in Warrington! All this is now tacitly ad, nitted lay the nubile proceedings of the Board Inert Fridny nkght, without one word of explanation, or r!gret. It is time that the Board caused notices of caution, sigiml by the Lae, Clerk, to be printed and posted on the walls, and disinfectants were freely used about the drains nod ashpits of infected places. But for all efficient practical purposes, the Law Clerk might as well I have whistled to the wird to take Ow lion away. The smal of the infection was in the human bodice of the patients, and note the ash-pits and drains, though no doubt ash-pita and drains ire DA condition are great fertilisers of the fever poison. And re! methods stopping abort of the separation of the infected patient from the healthy members of the family ere comparatively use- less, and can only end in bringing all sanitary regulations into disc.rwlit with the .commion people.

The ash-pit, drain, and sewer onestion in Lynim no doubt shoold he attended to. fir. Fox keen,., good deal about it, foot more than anybaly else. Why has the Board allowed to many cottages in Statham to be occupied by the labour- ing e.t.a, without pure water and without autlicient drainage for Om purport. of health and pinion, when t,e Board had the means in its own hands of enforcing all needful starlit try! regulations? And why did not It,. Fox, as Medical Officer I of Health, compel the Board to do its duty in this respect, if all quieter means proved ineffectual? For what does he receive hie large salary of 000 a year but to see that the ' Beard of Health in his dietrict do their duty ? If the doctor had spok. u with the %tow enero and determinaron in Ind al he did on last Friday night, the evil of which he spoke and to which he imperatively directed their attention, would have been r,in,ditebtlivtt, title I this need fal work been done in time, and the first Coßei of the present outbreak of scarlet fever been cent to the hospital, as soon as the presence of the disease was recognised ; it is as certain mc human probability can go, that the outbreak would have been at onceatopped in it, course, and no bereaved mother in Lymm would have had to mourn the net ~t her child.

Pot th;-doctor promises a special report on thr subject by and by. There is nothing now left us but to wait patiently for it, and see what crumb., of comfort it will afford lint don't let him forget to tell us—we will forgive every other omission he choomee to make—why it was, end let on have tne truth, the whole truth, and nothing hut the truth, about it—why it was that the first patients were not cent to the hospital P And does the doctor admit any peroonal respon- sibility of his OVin in the matter P—Yours faithfully, West View, Lyme,, March PI, ISSO. W. ROBSON.

THE GAME LAWS. Ste—Con you allow me space for a few words on this subjeet—The House of Commons rejected bye large major- ity on Tuesday Mr. P. A. Taylor'e motion for the abolition of the Game 'Laws. The tell-styled Farmers' Friends, the Tory English County Members, were, as in other ymrs, COII3piCLIOLIA in their interposition for the maintenance of a system of game protection which in more ways than one injures the farmer's husbandry, reduces the quality of his erops, and renders hie toil less prsii table. Mr.Tavlorassertmf, . strongly but truly, that there are ° no other laws like the Faiglish Game Laws in the civilisod world for though both France awl Gertnaity once had bows its bad, they were swept away IT the Revolutions of 1769 and 184., arid the fact remaitust that there were no Game Laws in the world which could be compared 10 00,1 for severity anal atrocity." Under these laws, 10,001 prosecutions occur in Engl..' every year, and many a poverty-stricken English mason, who has no chance of tasting flesh or fowl by purchase out of his scanty wage, goes to gaol amongst habitual thieves and scoundrels as the penalty for having trapped a hare or shot a pheasant The reason why our oppremive Ganie Laws have so longs life is perfectly apparent. A large pro- portion of the men sent to Parliament belong either to the landed aristocracy or to the indolent class, to whoni, in the Ammo of real productive work, sport is a necemity of ex- istence and on questions like this these gentry go to Par- liament to legislate for their own requirements, not for the interests of tenant farmers awl the public—to see that the game which afford,' them sport is jealously preserved by law, whatever becomes of awiculture and he ante.. workers. The lone of opinion o,e the Game Laws, as formed by these selfish personal considerations, amongst Members of the country party in the House, is indicated in the remarks of Sir W. Barttelot in moving an amendnient to Mr. Taylor's mmion, and of Earl Percy in seconding it; the latter said that the repeal of the Oaine Laos" would only destroy the attractiveness of country life." Perhaps it Is too much to expect, as English society and the British Houses of Legislature are at pre-sent constituted, the entire removal of the laws vrhich support game-preserving. Those portions of our higher moorlamls which are incapable of being turnwl into pasturage for cattle or meadow land, or even of being farmed as sheep runs, might he reserved as cover for birds which nestle in the heather, such . the grouse,. long as the ancient common rights of the neigh- bouring inhabitants to dig turf thereon are not interfered with. But with reganl to game which breeds and feeds in the most fertile lowlands, and particularly to ground game which is in so many cases the bane amt pest of the farmer, it is high time that legal protection tee its preservation was done away with. The debate in the House of Conimons on Tuesday was to some degree encouraging to those who wish In see our English fanners relieved from this incubus. Some Members who could not vote with Mr. Taylor for total repeal still insisted own speedy and material amendments of the Game Laws; for instance, Mr. C. S. Read, Sir A. Gonlon, and to,. Rodwell. And when, after the rejection of M. Taylor's motion, Sir William Harcourt moved then... sion of the word not" from Sir W. Barttelot.t awe ildnient, scan to make it raid, "that it is expedient at iiresent to deal with the qumtion of the Game Laws," notwithstanding Sir Stafford Nor-thecae's suggestion that Sir Wm. Harcourt , was only making fun of the business, there were no many supporters to Sir Wen. Harcourt that the suggested altera- tion wax only feet by 135 votes to 119, or a majority of 18. Public opinion is more than ripe for essential amendment of the Game Laws, and if the farmers who suffer most from them, in damage to land, tillage, fences, and crops, Rill have the courage to let their voices be hmrd in each of the county constituencies at the Geared Election in cotslemna- tion of these laws as they stand, they may expect to see them dealt with in an enlighten.' spirit by the next House of Commons. For Conservative e.didates I don't pre- tend to slowtk, but I do think that every Liberal candidate at the coming Election should be prepared to imke a drastic reform of the Cratne Laws an item in his political pro- gramme. It is one of several ellangen itidispenmble to the emablifinneet of a thoroughly eflicient, fully prothietive, and (to the farmer) fairly profitable system of agriculture In this eoantry.—Youre

Snot:Rum DisAsTalig TO VoLI,-rEEII °Mfr.-Y.—On Saturday afternoon a party of filmen officers of the Lanark- brigade of Artillery Volunteers, under the charge of Cap.ins and Adjntants Marsh and Wilson, lfoth of the Royal Artil- lery, and accompanied by Lieutenant-Colonel Commandant Kidson, proc,eded to their battery at Irvine, between twenty and thirty miles from Glasgow, for gun praCtice at the 40- pounder breachlotder. Sergeant.lnstructor Kirker, was putting a fuse into shell and gave it a stronger blow than usual with a mallet to drive it home. The result was ignition and immediate explosion. The sergeant-instructor was sewrely wounded about the head, arms, and borly. Lieut• Colonel West Watson had his left knee shatterel. Major Mathieson received a aevere concussion in the ed.- :mm,.hile the other six officers were more or less severely wounded. The sergeant.instructor died at midnight, having mode. voluntary declaration that he alone was responsible for the accident. It was found necessary to amputate Col. leg above the knee, but the loss of blood en weaken,' him that he flied at seven o'clock rfn Sunday morning. One or two of the other officers are severely wounded, but all are progressing favourably. Colonel Wat- son was a merchant in the cite, and fras the son of tte City Chamberlain. The Cemetery Coinmittee submitted a report front a sub- committee to the effect that over one acre and a half of land (common) had beon need for the interment of only one beffer en each grave, and that if this course is to be pursued ; thelurther extension of the cemetery will inn few years he Council:er HAMM,n moved and Councillor KRAW se- conded the adoption of the minutes. . . Councillor Hannteen said it was a sentiment which had been proved to be every absurd one indeed. If they or he had a grave at the Cemetery, and were unfortunate enough to lose five or six of their family, they could bury them all in one grave without any hesitation whatever. But in the common ground they were obliged. according to law, to keep a grave closed against the reception of any other body for fourteen years. It was passed for this purpose Suppoeing poor persons could not afford to buy a grave, but found themselves in subsequent nears better off, they could pur- chase the graves as famiir graves. He believed that had only been done in three instances dove the establishment of the Cemetery, which showed how absurd the regulation was. He was told in almost every cemetery within a considerable distance of Warrington they entirely ignored it. It would be recollected a ore.' hubbub wag made some years ago on it being discovered that they buried fear persona in one grave, but if they had not done so they would have had to extend tile cemetery considerably beyond its present limits, ! Mr. Knatchbutt-Hugeosen addressed the following letter recently to Mr. George Condelet, of Manchester :—My dear sir,—Yon wished me to embody in writing not views lee-. peCIIFIg the action of the licensed vietrilers' and brewing Mere,to tithe oorning general eh ction, and I do eo with much pleasure. In 1874 these interviste very generally united against the Liberal party. I think they dia tome degree beyond what was wise and right. For instance, I know of easee where the Liberal candidates had distinctly refused to vote for the Permissive Bill, and net" the tnnie,” ignoring the fact that their organisation we; prod:timed cote not p, be identified with either Janda party, but rest- ing man trade considerations only, adopted the Itny candi- dates, cool gave them the full benefit of their organised strength. At the sante tiine,in caste hoc ma own, anti...alit I was recognieed se deserving of support by' the trade," the only resolution passed by the loml node orgreisatlon that their friends should be advised to vote "according to their political convictione," lot only placing me mmu an equality with two new 'tory eanditheas, and giving 0000,0 trade support as such. The excuse bn this action hi 1074 of course, ttutt ',old Aberdare, then Mr. Bruce, bad, on Mr. Gladatim.'s Home :Secretary, Profs.., a h,lln 1,101, wan most obnoxious to the tratle,and which wano bilged to he withdrawn before its second reading owing to the unpopu• larity which im provisions not unnaturally excited. All persons cannected with the trade non, smarting wads, the attack which they considered to have been 111.10 011/011 0011 by the Liberal Government, and they took 00007 complete revenge by playing into the hands jf the Tory party no great number of constituencies The case, however, is widely different to-day, and I feel very strongly that a repetition of the course taken iu 1874 will be. great mistake. In saying this I put altogeth, . r ide the consideration which, as a Liberal, appears 10 101.' of grant weight—namely, that, inasmuch as the publicans , throughout the country murt depend for their Orostwiity 0010010 the ability of the trading and wage-earning classes to deal with theml the party which increases tlml ability by advocating a peaceful foreign policy and those domesßc j improvements which bring to these classes brisk trade, maid , Wages, and plenty of employnient must be the party whnee ; predominance im most to be desired both by publicans and , all other trades. I put this. I say, aaide for the moment, , because I want to consider Ple qu;otion from another point of view—namely, ham that in which I think it should pre- nent 11.011 10 'teemed victuallefs with reference to the dan- • gets which they believe threaten them at thin moment. Now, what are those dingers? Al the root of them all lies t this—the attempt to identify licensed victuallers with the , evila arising from intemperance. You will not misunderstand me. I have always resisted , thia attempt. I maintain that if you have a regulated trade , those to whom it is entrained are not persons to be looked I upon with suspicion and treated as if it was their object to MlSContluet thet trade, but that, under proper regulations of I amuse, they should he trusted to cony on their business , with ae little interference as possible. But the evils of intemperance having been generally ad- , mitted, note strong desire to repress and minimise them having sprung up in the public mind, it appears to me that the real danger 'shich mos' threatens the trade is their pm- , slide identification with these evils. And if the action of j the trade at the coming election is not cautious and well- , adviaed, this identification will be certain, and its comae. , quenees most diamtroun to their interests. The report of , the House of Lords' Committee has stimulant, public , opinion in this matter, and the main object which the trade , should have it to prevent that public opinion from being directed into • channel (an might easily be the ease) a. injur not to themselves. The talk about °'l i ocal option" s only a one phase of a growing public opinion. flit no rise to deny a the fact, and it is. moreover, foolish to do so, especially as the objections to the prment proposal of " local option," as a understand it, are objections quite apart from and indepen- dent Iti trade considerations. If the trade persist in demand- i leg pittages from mndidates to vote for or against particula,- measures, and if they throw their organisation into the wale , against Liberal candidates who refuse such pledgee, the in- u fallible and not very distant result ill be that they will I turn against themselves the full force and weight of the c growing public opinion against intemperance: they will a force the Liberal party, as a party, to aide with that public I Opinion and they will regret, when too late, that they have c suffered themselves to be entrapped into beeoming (practi. catty) pothical partisans. You will naturally ask me what course I think the trade , ought to take. I reply that, in the first place. the necessity ; for their taking any definite course as a trade is lees than in 1874, bemuse their action in that year has mused their ! tluence and importance to be no generally recognised that there is little fear of an attack by either political party upon their vented interests or man choir legitimate position unless t they unwisely and unnecessarily exasperate a pirty which, in the nature of things, must sooner or later come into power. I would advise them to profess—that which I no, sure they feel—an equal desire with all other right-thinking people to check intetnperance, and a readiness to allow fair considera- don Many proposal mode for that object. Further, I would , advise them 10000 w their confidence (which, 1t,,, sure, is I well grounded) that Parliament will not allow any unfair 7 attacks upon their interests to succeed, and their reliance a upon the good sense and feeling of statesmen on both sides , of the House. In this spirit I would have them counsel I their friends to vote acconling to their political opinions in every constituency, and not lot a moment when the neon,- City'doee not exist) snake themselves unpopular inn trade a comoination by identifying themselves with one, and acting in avowed hostility to the other political party. Moreover, although I do not with to say anything of my political opponents, I would have yon beer in mind a that, as in the case of the extension of the fronchise and other questions, the antecedents of the lory party hav,. shown that wheu public opinion taints decidedly in one , direction previous pledges and votes do not prevent thein I from shaping their course in the line to indicateth It may. . therefore, happen that atiould the action of the trade mot.° , against them a public opinion which is just now in a very doubtful state upon all miestions affecting the liquor traffic , they may find the very tarty whom they support turning, round man them in order to meet the demands of t at I pulilic opinion. To my mind, therefore. their wisest and mast prudent , course is In stand well aloof from any organiution, to rote as individruds according to theb political views, and so to maintain their independent pennon that questions affecting their trade may la considered impartially hymen of both political parties. AnviL Cuattrmr Smut°. As Sr. TIELMIB.—The annual charity sermons in aid of the schools in connection with the Church of the Sacred Heart, were preachwl on Sun- day last, by the Rev. Father Murphy, of St. Anthony's Church, Liverpool. High Mans was celebrated at eleven o'clock in the morning, the Rev. Father O'Reilly officiating. Father Murphy took for hie teat, "To him that giveth on wiodorn will give glory" (Ecclesienten). After briefly referring to the object that brought hint an.onget them, he proceeded to place before the congregation the life of St. Thomas Aquinas, who, feast day it no, Setting forth his work on earth as an example fitting for all to follow. The greatest gift in life which thsl could give to man was that of genius of a high order, and the greatest and noblest effort which man bleared with that genius could give hack to his Maker was the development of that genius, and devoting it to the spreading of the knowledge and glory of religion. They were all impelled by s natural impulse to worship genius, and to admire those who cultivated learning, in whatever sphere they Might be placed is the world. There was no more 'ecrul shrine of genies than the Catholic Church. Her hand had been raised to blemand consecrate genius, and she had lifted up those whom she had consecrated that they might surroirld her altar, and that her light might go forth from her nanctuarv, spreading over every laud and every sea. To spread the knowledge of tiod wax the highest and holiest duty inan could Wier to his Maker. Wisdom was most useful, because it elevated them above that world. With meat purity id life there Ins always gnat genius, and there was never great genius without great punty and chas. tity. 'lle rev. ptwicher portrayed the life of St. Thomas, drawing the lessons that might be learned from if, and urged them to follow his stem, by imitating his virtue.. To attain greatness they must he virtuous, for it was only their virtues that made then, great in this world, and earned them the crown in the everlasting kingdom. There were large congregitions at both services. The music, an usual, was rendered by the juvenile choir, Min Farrell officiating at the harmonium.

The Maxon said : Before formally opening this exhibition perhaps you will expect me to say a word or two and I may say that I do it at the kind invitation of the Chairman of the Ulu Cotninitttee. I quite agree with hint, and with the members of the committee, that it was very desirable that an exhibition of this kind should take Mace. We have had the great exhibitions of Paris and London, and exhibi- tions also in various other parts of the globe, and I may aly that they have tendnt to the advantage and to the interests of this country. I may say alto that the farmers of this country have their exhibitions annually ; for we see they displayed the various implemenm in connec- tion with husbandry. I may say with respect to to this exhibition that it has been of great interest to those connected with farming in this country. I will candidly confess that I believe the m.dive that both the chairman a the committee and the committee themselves have in hold- ing this exhibition is with the object of increasing the con- sumption of gas; and they have thrown this building open Ito those who wish to exhibit here, and allow me to express the wish awl the hope that the exhibition may be of adv.- ' tage to the committee and to the Corporation, and that it : may be advantageous to the exhibitors theinselves—(hear , hearl—and to those who purchase. (Hear, hear.) Now vou are aware, unwell as I am, of the season which is now 'approaching, when the heat is almost unbearable in our houses it consequence of having fires for cooking purposes. , With respect to some of them stoves which are exhibited here to-day. I will venture to say that they will be of ad- vantage in this respect. I have seen them in operation my.' self, and after the cooking is dispensed with the gas may be turned off, and you mn get your kitchen comparatively cool. As I have said before. I hope it may result advan- tageously to all parties, and I now declare this exhibition open. (Applause.) To increase the interest in the exhibition, Mrs. Thwaitew the noted lecturer on cookery, gave a dernenetrative lecture at four o'clock to an intelligent audience, compowd mostly of ladies.

Mr. Coot said that in the alwence of the Mayor he was asked to introduce Mrs. Thwaites. The cooking would be done exclusively hy gas. The 6ao Consmittee thonght it would give the public an opportunity tot judging of the fa- cilities now offered for cooking and heating purpors hy gas; and it was thought by engagjog Mrs. Thwaites that it would enhance the interest felt in the exhibition.

Mrr. Tilwarrea then proceeded with her lectnre, which was thoroughly appreciated. Mrs. Thwaites is very explicit, and her skill in the art of cooking to admirable that no one could fail to understand bet meaning or appre- ciate her illustrations. At the commenceinent of her lecture she said that cooking by gas was very much cleaner and nicer than the ordiaary way, and she preferred it. She proceeded to make lentil soup, lobster cutlets, cold chicken ri..soles, a savoury omelet, and Queen's pudding, the virtues of which were tested by the audience, and pronounced excellent. We should not forget to mention the gas engines that were located downstairs. 'The "Otto" silent gas engine was shown by Messrs. Crossley lirothers,Great Marlborough- street, Manchester. It was half-horse power, and price LAO. The consumption of gas was 10 feet per hear, at the cost of ohout 0. per hour at the rate of 4s. per thousand cubic feet. Close to WAS exhibited one of Turner's potent gas engines, manufactured by the patentee, at St. Albans, England. The only apparent drawback in this engine was its great noise. cau.sed by the working of the shaft; and there was a great contrast between it and the almost noiseless working of the •• Otta " horizontal engine. A lesser engine, of two-m to power, called Iliuschop," was exhibited he Mn. E. J. Andrews. of Waterloo-road, Stockport. This is an engine of very simple construction, and will drive two large jobbing printing machines, is suitable for corn crushing, chaff cutting, drc.

Tn. LAWCISRIDE [now AND, Coo, Taanxs.—There is no very material change to notice in the condition of the coal trade throughout thia district since last week. The quantity of rountl coal of all descriptions offering in the market is still much iu excess of the demand, and stocks at the collieries are increasing, whilst the pits generally are being put on short time, many of them not ;working more than three to four days a week. Colliery proprietors gener- ally complain that the depression in trade is being felt quite as keenly as last minim, as the preparations made to meet the itnprovensent in trade, so confidently anticipated before the closing of last rear, but which has not been realised, have brought supplies into the market altogether beyond present requirements. There is a gast deal of irregularity in prices, but the average quotations at the pit mouth may he given about as under : Best Lancashire house coal, Is. M as. 6d.; second qualities, 6s. to 6s. 6.1.; and column. round coal for steam and forge purposes, fis. to to. 6d. per ton. For good slack at the pit mouth 35. Al. per tonic about the average price now asked, with lower qualities ranging from Pt. At. to 3s. per ton.—ln the iron trade of this district there is still only a limited inquiry either for home con- sumption or export, and the ceswition of the export demand has thrown some of the iron which had been bought on American account upon the home market. The consequence has been that oecond-hand iron has been offering at lower figures, north country brands especially having been obtain- able at considerably under last week's prices, and the busi- ness doing seems to 11,ve been confined chiefly to cheap lota of merchant iron. The lull, however, ia generally. only regarded as temporary, and makers, as • rule, bring in no immediate want of orders, are still very Into. The bulk of the local make of pig iron in still going away on account of ,Ad contract, and Lancashire welters, having very little iron to offer, do not quote under 70s. per ton. less 23/4 per cent. for delivery eqttal to Manchester. Second-hand lots of finished iron offering in the market beer lotil a tendency to weaken the price of hers, but good Lancashire qualities can- not be bought from makers under about £8 151. to £9 per ton, althongh there are parcels offering by merchanG for delivery equal to Manchester or Liverpool from £8 he, to £l3 10s, per ton. Hoops are generally firm at about late rates. ELECTION NOTES. Though everybody had been looking forward r, diewolution of Parliament, they had begun to snapset that the Premier wso bent upon sticking to the sweets ofoffiee until, by the elapse of time, the law itself should ,rist him and his. The announeement, therefore, in the House of Commons, on Monday afternoon, by the Chancellor of the Extheyner, that the Cabinet hod deeided to dissolve Parliament at Esator, crested surprise in the House iterlf, and as the &Aeration was flashed by telegraph from town to town, the whole country was, in a few hours, thrown Into ...gement. The Cabinet kept its secret well until the last moment ; and when the announc, went of its de•ermination to dissolve Parliament was given, everylev3y began to wonder why it had so sud- denly come to the decision. People , have to be content to pv, on wondering for a time; the "Mrs. tery Man," Lord Beaconsfield, veils the hidden motives of tbe Cabinet by the pretence that the a..- .lotion would have been heralded sooner hut for the Government's anxiety to assuage the distress which has loon, and in now, a wourge to Ireland but the " murder will out," and when the day of reckoning dooc come' as it aseuredly will, we shall not be surprised to learn that tho removal of the cloven hoof has revealed rottenness in the Beacons. fieldian Denmark.

There is a suspicion abroad that the failure of the Horne Secretary's London Water Bill has had much to do with hastening the resolution to dismlve PATElament. When it was discoverA that in the very hotbed of Jingoism the Government would raise a hornet's nest about their ears ,f they persisted in pnasing on with the Bill, it wan determined to drop the Bill as they would a hot potato, and cover the manmuvre with the proclaination of a dis-oluti.. A London corrrspondent remarks that alt is not pleasant to believe or to say that there has been any unfair d,iling M the matter of the London Water Bill, but there are rumours abroad so persistent, so precise, and so concordant, that anyone who reads them cannot hot be tilled by an uncomfortable suipicion that in some mysterious manner the cont,.ts of the bill became known to speculators almost as soon as the measure was drafted, and that the re- mit has been the realimtion of enornions surns by some of three forewarn.d persons. It ',this suspicion that they will, if tbe bill were to pass, be made victims of a gigantic job which more than anything else actuates the ratepayers in the most unmistakable hostility they have shown towards the meaaure, and which beyond question will lead them to insist that it shall be dropped, or at least no •Itered as to be no longer the same thing. If the secret has been allowed to leak out, it would, of course, be In spite of Mr. Cross's vigilance. He has, no slootn, tried to do the best he could, but he has nevertheless , made a miaerable muddle of the whole business, and haa thgeby straek blow at his own reputation from which it will not soon recover, especially as the right hon, gentleman' seem, to be unceasing of late in his endeavours to damage it further. Perhaps, even without .y effort on his part, his character aa a practical statesman is doomed. A man cannot live for ever on a reputation derived front an Artisans' Dwellings Act which does not work." Our facetious contemporary, Punch, attributes the death of Parliament to the failure of the Water Bill, and has pre- pared the following epitaph commemorative of ita decease:—

Though the dissolution was expected by some of the princi- pal Liberals in the town, many of the frequenters of the club seemed a little astonished at (betiding,, and could not refrain from vigorously exercising their lungs. div.p: motation of South Went Lanc.tehiro, of which St. Helene

forms a part. Ehe Liberals have divided the town into four • districts, the Windle, Eccleston, Sutton, and Parr, ; and that of Rainforil makes five. Meetings of committees are being held in various parts of the town. Mr. H. S. Hall is chair. man of the Windle Committee, and Mr. Richard Pilkington of the Eceleston Committee.

A meeting of the Parr Committee was held on Thursday night, and at the same time another meeting was held at Eceleston, to prepare the necessary arrangements for a con- teet The greatest unanimity exists on the Liber.sl side, and there will be nO lack of voluntary workers to secure the suc- cessful return of the Liberal candidates. Thie is most gratifying, and it is to be hoped that this harmony will prevail throughout the contest. The secretaries of the Eceleston Committee are Messrs. Rowlinson and It. Lowe. The Sutton Committee ha alte held meetings. and in all probability canvassing throughout the town will bec,in to- ' day (Saturday.) The electoral campaign was also begun on Tueeday, Cl SatabpOrt. At the last election it will be re- thembered the fight con, nenced alien. Helens, no far as the holding of great public meetings went. The Southport Committee have been hard at work, nod they guarantee they will have fully a majority of 701) for the Liberal candidate. The secretary of the Liberal Club visited Rainford, on Thureday, with a view to induce the Liberals in that town- ship to prepare for the coming contest.

Who are to be the Liberal candidates for South-West Lancashire has not been definitely decided. The Conser- vative candidates will be the present members, the Rigltt Hon. R. A. Cross and Colonel J. Ireland Blackburn. The Liberals, however, are well organised in the division, and a soon as arrang, mem., with respect to candidates, have been settled they will he telly prepared for engaging in a straggle jet which they have an excellent prospect of achieving sue- ce.s. It is understaxl that one of the Litterat can- didatee will be rho Hon. Mr. Molineux, brother to the Earl of Seq., and Colonel Gamble has been mentioned ae his probable colleague. There is a desire, however, to induce Mr. Rathbone, the Liberal Member for Liverpool, to consent to be put in nomination along with the Hon. Mr. Idolineaux.and a depu- tation has been sent frnm Liverpool to London to wait upon! him with that object. Ills expectcal that at meeting in ' Liverpool (to be held to-night, Friday) Mr Rothbone's reply will be received, and that • definite course of action will em decided upon.

Parliament, according to the statement of the (*owellor of the Exchequer, will rise on the rd instant. On the 24th the disnolution will be proclaimed by the Queen, and on the same day writs, which are said to be in readiness, will be lensed for • new election. On the 25th the writs will be in the hands of moat, if not all, the returning officers throughout the kingdom. The Parliamentary Elections Act, 1872, requires that in counties and district boroughs notice should he given of the day of election within two days after the receipt of the writ. The election must then be fixed for not later than the ninth day after the receipt of the writ, audit the seat Iceconteeted a poll must be taken at an interval of not less than two, nor more than nix, clear days after that fixed forth< election. In boroughsnot being district boroughs, the returning oflicer must give notice of the election on the day or the day alter the writ arrivra, and must fix it for not later than the fourth day after the receipt of the writ, the poll being taken not more than three clear days after the day appointed for the election. Assuming, therefore, that the majority of the writs will reach the respective returning officers by Thursday, March 25th, the borough elections it these caeca must be appointed at the latest for Wednesday,. the 3leo. As Friday, beteg flood Friday, is dire non, the earliest pomade day on which the poll can be taken is flutter Monday, the 29th.

The following letter was read from the Local Government Board, dated 6th March Sir,-1 arc directed by the LOVA Government Board to forward to the Guardians of the Warrington Union the accompanying plans for the pro- posed new schools at Fatima., which bave been submitted to the Board by Messrs. Fierpoint and Sun, tlte Guardians' architects ; and PISO tIIC enclosed architectural notes setting forth certain particulars in which the plans appear capable of amendment. Mr. Fierpoint bee had a conference with the Board's architect w lb regard to the plans, and he will In able to explain more folly the points raised in the notes. Generally speaking, the ;dans appear to he well designed, but the Board are very anxious that while every arrangement is made to promote health and efficiency in theschools, all need- less expenditure shood be avoided. Thowater tower, steam en- gine, and the tower to the schools could probably be omit- ted ; and as good water is said to be reached at little depth, a pump for each house 'night he found sufficient to give an ample supply. Some difficult questions will arise respecting the administration of the schools, and perhaps it would save trouble lithe Chairman awl Vice-Chairomn could discuss I them in London. The overflow of the drains cannot be I allowed ache discharged into the stream."—The "notes" .- 1 conmanying the letter contained the following :—" It is to 1 he observed that no provision is contemplated by the plans for the treatment, on the site, of sick children.
