Mr. (Menage thought the case a very serious one. Mr. Samuel Henry Hartley was then called, and said he lived in the township of Eccleston. Up to the 23rd Augual he was relieving officer and collector to the Guardians for the WidlleS district. In consequence of some information which came to Ids knowledge, he came to Widnes on the 23rd August, and went to the place where it was usual forthe poor people to receive their pay, and found that Fowler had left the place and waa nowhere to let found. He next went to the prisoner's house and took Nasession of his hooks. He then found that one of the Guardians of the poor—Mr. Carlile—had obtained morev with which to pay the people who were in receipt of relief. Mr. Carlile end Mr. Matthews (another guardian) then proceeded to pay the poor at the pay station—the Volunteer Hall—and heassisted them. He Ascertained that the £25 had been drawn by the prisoner. armunt of the Prescot Union. The prisoner would not receive the cheque from the Board of Guardians, hut, as a matter of fact, her ime to his office, at one o'clock on the afternoon of the 25h August, and obtained the cheque for £25. It was an order upon the treasurer. and would be signed by the Chairman of the Board and two other inenthers. The cheque was clabol the 14th August, and he did not give it the pimner personally. The practice was to send themheques toy post the day before they were needed. The prisoner got the cheque eathed at Pore's Bank. The Guardians 113113 special cheque or order book.and the cheque was an order in question upon Mr. Chrimes to pay to the order of any person directed by the Guardians. He could not say from his own knowledge what the practice of Mr. Fowler was. The consolidated orders required that an vidual should he named as a treasurer, and not a firm. On visiting the prisoner'. house, he found that his wife was preparing to leave, and knew nothing of Ids whereabouts. Ile took pomession of the books belonging to the union, and aniongst them was the one dealingwith receipt and expendi- ture. The £25 was given to the prisoner in order that he might make certain payments, hut in the case of discharging tradesmen'. accouno other cheques would be given to him. The average Hie( in Widnes was about £24. It was Pow- !2l'% duty ho enter the amounts up. Be' Inspector Barnett: In addition to thin deficiency, have you found any other? The auditor certified to some den. ciencies.—Did you fled them yourself? I have not to find them that is the duty of the auditor. - .

Mr.bpeneolyeoiditoeoe quite clear that the evidence with regard to the various sums of which the £25 consisted had not been worked up to completion. Witness said he could that day produce the whole of the evidence he should be able to offer and. after come further explanations by him, the hearing was adjeurned to Thurs- day morning next, at ten o'clock. When-the letter from Mr. howler was put in evidence the clerk to the magistrates handed it to Mr. Gossage. and did not read it. At the end of the proceedings he pun- ned the somewhat Extraordinary Course of not read- ing over the deposition* so that it was impossible for the representatives of the peers to take a note of the communication. He. the reporters salting Mr. Spencely to kindly parmit tt.ent to see the letter, he in very gruff tone positively refused to do so. We are, however, happy to be able to Worm our readers that the communication contained an expreasion of sincere regret from the prisoner at the dis- grace which he had brought upon himself and family, and a request that he might be mercifully dealt with by the Guar- dians. He promised that if he was mercifully treated In would leave the country, with his wife and family, and go , Income foreign clime, where, under sunnier skies. he would try to lead a new life, and to stow there was still truth in Ithe old proverb that it woe neva too late to mend.

The following letter was read from the Local Government Board, dated 2611 t February I am directed by the Local Government Board to state that they have had under their consideration the report made by their inspector, Major Tub I lock, after the inquiry held by hint relative to the applica- Lion of the Town Council of St. Helens for sanction to bor- row £27,000 for works of water supply, and £7.348 for works of street improvements, and as to the objections to the proposed works of water supply which have been re- ceived by the Town Council. It appears that the Town Council with a view to increase the supply of water to thel borough so auto provide for the future requrements, propose to sink a well at Cronton, and that objection has been taken to the scheme on the ground that the work, if carried out, would act-lonely diminish the quantity of water furnished by wells already existing at, or in the neighbourhood of that place, on which the Widnes Local Board tad others depend for a water supply. The Board are aware from Major Tullocks's report of the representations made at the enquiry on behalf of the Town Council, and the objections with respect to the scheme, and they have given this their care- ful attention. Having regard to the injurious effect which flee proposed works may probably have on the works of the Widnes Usual Board, and perhaps on the other wells at or near Croat., the Board are unable, as at present advised, to approve of the scheme. They are of opinion, therefore, that the Town Council should consider whether the supply of water they are likely to require cinnot be obtained ham some other source auto which a similar objection would not apply. I am directed to add that the Board are not aware of any objection to the proposed works of street improve- ment. and their sanction to the loan required for these works will shortly be forwarded.—l ani. sir, roar obedient servant. There sewers enter the brook at Bridgewater-street. In to sampl. of Hardshaw Brook furnished by Inspector Houghton. taken at ratio. pl.es, I find a faint acid in all tho.l from Laugtree neighbourhood. There is • slight trace of acid in the water of the pool at the Metal Extracting I Company's works. Sutton Brook is free, and Raiadord Brook hue no acid. There is acid in the samplee taken from the drain in Atlaacourt. There is no acid in .nal samples. At the lag meeting of this committee I repotted • nuisance at Gotten, alleged to exist in the neigh-1 bourhood of the Copper Works, said to consist of a gas of a ' suffocating nature. I have made almost daily visits to the works for the last five weeks, but have not found the es.pe of gas to hero free as to constitute a nuisance. I have hen shown through the works hr the manager, and am of opinion that they are at present conducted carefully. Those who live in the vicinity of them works admit that the nuisance they complained of has Oct existed of late, and that it arm in the foggy weather the gae b.arne obnoxious.'
